title: Sorting: Selection Sort
oneLiner: Repeatedly find the smallest remaining value and swap it into place -- the opposite instinct from bubble sort's constant neighbor-swapping.
keyTakeaway: Selection sort is O(n^2) like bubble and insertion sort, but for a different reason: it always does a full scan every pass to find the minimum, regardless of how sorted the input already is -- it can't finish early the way insertion sort can. In exchange, it makes at most n swaps total (one per pass), far fewer than bubble sort's swap-on-every-out-of-order-pair approach -- useful when swaps (not comparisons) are the expensive operation.
explanation: For each index i starting at 0, scan the entire remaining unsorted slice [i..n-1] to find the index of its SMALLEST value -- then, after the scan finishes, swap that minimum into position i. After processing index i, [0..i] holds the i+1 smallest values in sorted order, done for good. Watch out for the common shortcut bug: swapping immediately every time you find a smaller value during the scan, instead of tracking the minimum's INDEX and doing exactly one swap at the end of the pass -- the immediate-swap version still happens to sort correctly, but it's not selection sort's actual algorithm (and does needless extra swaps).

visualizationSteps.message: Starting array: [5, 2, 4, 1, 3]. Each pass finds the minimum of the remaining unsorted slice and swaps it into place.
Pass 1: scan [0..4] for the smallest value. Start assuming index 0 (value 5) is the min.
arr[1]=2 < current min 5 -- new min index is 1.
arr[2]=4 >= current min 2 -- min index stays 1.
arr[3]=1 < current min 2 -- new min index is 3.
arr[4]=3 >= current min 1 -- min index stays 3.
Swap index 0 with the found minimum -> [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]. Index 0 is now in its final sorted position.
Pass 2: scan [1..4] for the smallest value. Start assuming index 1 (value 2) is the min.
arr[2]=4 >= current min 2 -- min index stays 1.
arr[3]=5 >= current min 2 -- min index stays 1.
arr[4]=3 >= current min 2 -- min index stays 1.
Index 1 was already the minimum -- no swap needed. Index 1 is now in its final sorted position.
Pass 3: scan [2..4] for the smallest value. Start assuming index 2 (value 4) is the min.
arr[3]=5 >= current min 4 -- min index stays 2.
arr[4]=3 < current min 4 -- new min index is 4.
Swap index 2 with the found minimum -> [1, 2, 3, 5, 4]. Index 2 is now in its final sorted position.
Pass 4: scan [3..4] for the smallest value. Start assuming index 3 (value 5) is the min.
arr[4]=4 < current min 5 -- new min index is 4.
Swap index 3 with the found minimum -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Index 3 is now in its final sorted position.

complexity.note: Always scans the whole unsorted remainder to find the minimum -- n²/2 comparisons no matter how the input is ordered.
